title: Resistance to Apartheid in the 1950s
summary: The ANC Youth League and the Programme of Action, the Defiance Campaign, the Freedom Charter, the 1956 Women's March and the Treason Trial.

notes.text: The **African National Congress (ANC)**, founded in 1912, had at first used petitions and deputations. In **1944** young members including **Nelson Mandela**, **Walter Sisulu**, **Oliver Tambo** and **Anton Lembede** formed the **ANC Youth League**, which called for more direct, mass action. In **1949** the ANC adopted the Youth League's **Programme of Action**: boycotts, strikes, civil disobedience and non-cooperation.

The ANC and the **South African Indian Congress** launched the **Defiance Campaign against Unjust Laws** on **26 June 1952**. Volunteers deliberately broke apartheid laws, for example using 'whites only' entrances, being in town after curfew or not carrying passes, and allowed themselves to be arrested peacefully.

items: ANC membership grew from about 7 000 to about 100 000.
The government responded with harsher laws and heavier penalties for protest.
The campaign followed Gandhi's ideas of **passive resistance**.

notes.text: The Congress of the People and the Freedom Charter, 1955

The **Congress Alliance** (the ANC, the SA Indian Congress, the Coloured People's Congress, the white Congress of Democrats and the SA Congress of Trade Unions) asked people across the country to send in their demands. On **26 June 1955**, about 3 000 delegates met at **Kliptown**, Soweto, at the **Congress of the People** and adopted the **Freedom Charter**.

notes.title: Source H: Extract from the Freedom Charter, 1955
notes.text:
We, the People of South Africa, declare for all our country and the world to know: that South Africa belongs to all who live in it, black and white, and that no government can justly claim authority unless it is based on the will of all the people.

The People Shall Govern!
All National Groups Shall have Equal Rights!
The People Shall Share in the Country's Wealth!
The Land Shall be Shared Among Those Who Work It!
All Shall be Equal Before the Law!
All Shall Enjoy Equal Human Rights!
There Shall be Work and Security!
The Doors of Learning and Culture Shall be Opened!
There Shall be Houses, Security and Comfort!
There Shall be Peace and Friendship!

notes.label: Key idea
notes.text: Many ideas in the Freedom Charter, such as equality before the law and the right to education, are found in South Africa's **Constitution of 1996**.

When the government announced that black women would also have to carry passes, the **Federation of South African Women** (FEDSAW) organised a march. About **20 000 women** of all races, led by **Lilian Ngoyi**, **Helen Joseph**, **Rahima Moosa** and **Sophia Williams-De Bruyn**, marched to the **Union Buildings** in Pretoria. They left petitions for Prime Minister Strijdom and stood in silence for 30 minutes, then sang:

*Wathint' abafazi, wathint' imbokodo* ('You strike the women, you strike a rock').
9 August is now celebrated as **National Women's Day**.

In December 1956 police arrested **156 leaders** of the Congress Alliance, including Mandela, Sisulu, Tambo, Albert Luthuli and Helen Joseph, and charged them with **high treason**, claiming that the Freedom Charter was a communist plan to overthrow the state by violence. The trial dragged on for more than four years, but in **1961** all the accused were found **not guilty**.

Other resistance in the 1950s included the **Alexandra bus boycott** (1957), when thousands walked up to 30 km a day rather than pay higher fares, and rural uprisings such as in **Sekhukhuneland** and **Pondoland** against the Bantu Authorities system.
